2.text: in the light, either in the sleeping-room or in the outer tent, and even in

3.text: the daytime. Some are done clumsily enough; others, on the contrary, display

4.text: wonderful skill, which would do credit to a prestidigitateur of the first rank

5.text: in civilized countries. I must mention, moreover, that I had no chance of

6.text: meeting a shaman of the first rank, — a man of such ability that, in the words

7.text: of the Chukchee, “his renown would fully equal that of the ancient people,”

8.text: because shamans like that are not to be met with every day in modern times.

9.text: One Eskimo shaman of Uñiˊsak at Indian Point enjoyed a great repu-

10.text: tation in the surrounding country; and his neighbors, desirous of explaining

11.text: to me his great strength, said that he was like a keˊlᴇ, and that they were

12.text: afraid of him, as we Russians are afraid of the Sun Chief (Czar).¹ To

13.text: my regret he died a year before I reached Indian Point. Mr. Gondatti

14.text: certainly had an opportunity of meeting him, though he does not mention

15.text: him in his papers. I met only his wife, Uˊpuñe, who acknowledged that she

16.text: had acquired only a small part of his great art. Some of the feats effected

17.text: by her were, however, quite wonderful. For instance, while we were sitting

18.text: in the inner room of her house, with the lamps burning, she took the drum,

19.text: and, after practising on it for a little while, passed over to the characteristic

20.text: cries and violent motions ascribed to the keˊlet, thus conveying to us that

21.text: one of them had entered her body.

22.text: After that she took a large round pebble of the size of a man’s fist,

23.text: set it upon the drum, and, blowing upon it from all sides, began to mumble

24.text: and snort in the same keˊlᴇ-like manner. She called our attention with signs, —

25.text: being in the possession of the keˊlᴇ, she had lost the faculty of human

26.text: speech, and then began to wring the pebble with both hands. Then a

27.text: continuous row of very small pebbles began to fall from her hands. This

28.text: lasted for fully five minutes, till quite a heap of small pebbles was gathered

29.text: below, on the skin. The larger pebble, however, remained smooth and

30.text: intact, as was quite natural that it should be.

31.text: I sat quite close to the juggler, and followed attentively all her move-

32.text: ments, and I could not discover where all these pebbles came from. She

33.text: wore the usual combination-suit of women of that country, but the broad

34.text: waist was thrown open together with the sleeves; and all the upper part of

35.text: her body, including arms and hands, was quite naked, and accessible to

36.text: inspection. After a few moments I suddenly requested Uˊpuñe to repeat the

37.text: trick, meaning to try if I could not catch her unawares; but she immediately

38.text: took up her stone, and without more ado wrung out of it a stream of small

39.text: pebbles still larger than the first.

40.text: Another of her tricks referred to the special methods used by shamans

41.text: in their magic medicine. They pretend to be able to rip up with the knife
